In node2vec, homophily and structural equivalence are two different notions of what it means for nodes to be “similar.”

Homophily means that nearby nodes in the graph tend to be similar because they are directly connected or lie in the same local neighborhood. In embedding terms, a method that emphasizes homophily tries to place adjacent or close-by nodes near each other in the learned vector space.

Structural equivalence means that nodes are similar because they play the same role in the network, even if they are not directly connected. For example, two nodes can be structurally equivalent if they have similar connection patterns to other nodes, such as both acting as hubs or both serving as peripheral connectors in different parts of the graph.

node2vec uses biased random walks to generate node neighborhoods, and the BFS/DFS tradeoff controls whether those walks behave more like local neighborhood exploration or more like role-based exploration.

A BFS-like sampling strategy stays close to the starting node and repeatedly explores nearby nodes. This tends to preserve local proximity, so it is better aligned with homophily.

A DFS-like sampling strategy moves farther away from the starting node and explores nodes that may be structurally similar but not necessarily close in the graph. This makes it more suitable for capturing structural equivalence.

So, in short: BFS in node2vec biases the walk toward homophily, while DFS biases it toward structural equivalence. The method interpolates between these behaviors using its walk parameters rather than using pure BFS or pure DFS.
